Turpitude

TUR-pih-tood · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Turpitude is wickedness or shameful moral corruption.

The prosecutor called the scheme 'a textbook case of moral turpitude,' arguing the defendant had known exactly how much harm he was causing.

Worked Example

Legal scholars still argue over which crimes truly rise to the level of moral turpitude.

The debate is specifically about which acts count as deeply wicked or corrupt in a formal, almost legal sense -- exactly what turpitude names.

How Turpitude Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

depravity

depravity: moral corruption or degeneracy

wickedness

wickedness: the quality of being evil

Antonyms

virtue

virtue: moral excellence or goodness

integrity

integrity: adherence to strong moral principles

How Strong Is It? — misconduct → turpitude → depravity

misconduct vs. turpitude

misconduct vs. turpitude: Misconduct can mean any wrongdoing, mild or serious; turpitude specifically names conduct that is deeply, shockingly wicked.

depravity vs. turpitude

depravity vs. turpitude: Depravity and turpitude are close in strength, though turpitude carries a more formal, almost legal ring, especially in the fixed phrase 'moral turpitude.'

Build the Word

The pieces

root — turpi

root — turpi: vile, disgraceful (Latin (turpis))

suffix — -tude

suffix — -tude: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Turpitude comes directly from Latin turpis, 'vile, disgraceful,' plus the noun-forming -tude -- but turpis itself never became a standalone modern English word, so no root chip is quizzed here.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin turpis, 'vile, disgraceful,' never became an English word on its own, so turpitude has no root relative for you to find. The word simply bottles that Latin adjective inside the noun ending -tude, 'state or quality of.'

Strength Check

Word Choice

Turpitude has a distinctly formal, almost legal register -- it appears constantly in the fixed phrase 'moral turpitude' in court rulings and immigration law. In everyday, non-legal contexts, a plainer word like depravity or wickedness usually fits better.
